There were also Cui Chengzong, Yang Xie, Chen You, and Cui Qing—all because they upheld obedience were hated by rebels; Li Wenhui called them Gao Mu's faction. When Mu suffered harm, Chengzong and the others were likewise imprisoned and released. Guo Guang's fame was second to Mu's; though he did not die he fully tasted hardship and humiliation. When Liu Wu pacified the rebels he swiftly summoned Li Gongdu and grasped his hand, sighing. Once appointed Huazhou military commissioner he first recruited Guang and Gongdu as staff members.
104
元和十四年四月，詔曰：
In the fourth month of the fourteenth year of Yuanhe an edict said:
105
圖難忘死，為臣之峻節； 顯忠旌善，有國之令猷。 日者妖豎反覆，侮我朝章，而濮州刺史高沐，劫在兇威，潛輸忠款。 諷其不庭之咎，將冀革心； 數其煮海之饒，聿求利國。 伏奏必陳於逆節，漏師常破其陰謀。 竟以盜憎，遂死王事，歿而不朽，風聲凜然。 式表漏泉之澤，且彰勁草之節。 可贈吏部尚書。 仍委馬總訪其遺骸，以禮收葬，優恤其家。 若有子孫，具名聞奏。
Facing difficulty and forgetting death is a minister's stern integrity; displaying loyalty and signaling goodness is a state's fine plan. Recently the wicked villain reversed and repeated, insulting our court statutes; yet Puzhou Prefect Gao Mu, seized in villainous might, secretly conveyed loyal sincerity. Admonishing his fault of insubordination, he hoped to reform the heart; counting the riches of boiling sea, he sought benefit for the state. Secret memorials always stated rebellious conduct; leaking plans he often broke hidden conspiracies. Ultimately because robbers hated him he died in royal service—perished yet not decayed, reputation stern and clear. Thus showing the favor of the leaking spring and displaying the integrity of firm grass. He may be posthumously enfeoffed as minister of personnel. Still entrust Ma Zong to seek his remains, bury them with rites, and generously comfort his family. If there are descendants, report their names in full.
106
賈直言
Jia Zhiyan
107
賈直言者，父道沖，以伎術得罪，貶之，賜鴆於路。 直言偽令其父拜四方，辭上下神祗，伺使者視稍怠，即取其鴆以飲，遂迷仆而死。 明日鴆泄於足而復蘇。 代宗聞之，減父死，直言亦自此病蹙。 後從事於李師道。 師道不恭朝命，直言冒刃說者二，輿櫬說者一。 師道訖不從。 及劉悟斬師道，節制鄭滑，得直言於禁錮之間，又嘉其所為，因奏置幕中。 後遷於潞，亦與之俱行。 悟纖微乖失，直言必盡理箴規，以是美譽日聞於朝。 穆宗以諫議大夫征之，悟拜章乞留，復授檢校右庶子、兼御史大夫，依前充昭義軍行軍司馬。 悟用其言，終身不虧臣節。 後歷太子賓客。 太和九年三月卒，廢朝一日，贈工部尚書。
Jia Zhiyan—his father Daochong, because of skill in arts offended, was demoted and given poison on the road. Zhiyan falsely ordered his father to bow to the four directions, bidding farewell to spirits above and below; when the envoy's gaze slackened slightly he took the poison and drank it, then fell insensible as if dead. The next day the poison passed from his feet and he revived. Emperor Daizong heard and reduced his father's death; from this Zhiyan also had a limping illness. Later he served on Li Shidao's staff. Shidao was disrespectful of court orders; Zhiyan braved blades to admonish twice and once admonished bearing his coffin. Shidao to the end did not follow. When Liu Wu beheaded Shidao and governed Zheng and Hua he obtained Zhiyan from imprisonment and also praised his conduct, memorializing to place him on staff. Later transferred to Lu, he went together with him. Whenever Wu had the slightest fault Zhiyan always fully reasoned and admonished; thereby good reputation daily reached court. Emperor Muzong summoned him as remonstrance official; Wu submitted a memorial begging to retain him, again appointing him acting right vice mentor and concurrently censor-in-chief, continuing as Zhaoyi army acting marshal. Wu used his words and to the end did not fail ministerial integrity. Later he served as mentor of the Heir Apparent. In the third month of the ninth year of Taihe he died; court was suspended one day and he was posthumously enfeoffed as minister of works.
108
庾敬休
Yu Jingxiu
109
庾敬休，字順之，其先南陽新野人。 祖光烈，與仲弟光先，祿山迫以偽官，皆潛伏奔竄。 光烈為大理少卿，光先為吏部侍郎。 父河，當賊泚盜據宮闕，與季弟倬逃竄山谷。 河終兵部郎中。
Yu Jingxiu, styled Shunzhi, was originally a native of Xinye in Nanyang. His grandfather Guanglie, with his second younger brother Guangxian, when Lushan forced them into false office both hid and fled. Guanglie was vice director of the Court of Judicial Review; Guangxian was vice director of the Ministry of Personnel. His father He, when rebel Zhu Ci seized the palace, fled with his youngest younger brother Zhuo to mountain valleys. He finally served as director in the Ministry of War.
110
敬休舉進士，以宏詞登科，授秘書省校書郎，從事宣州。 旋授渭南尉、集賢校理。 遷右拾遺、集賢學士。 歷右補闕，稱職，轉起居舍人，俄遷禮部員外郎。 入為翰林學士，遷禮部郎中，罷職歸官。 又遷兵部郎中、知制誥。 丁憂，服闋，改工部侍郎，權知吏部選事，遷吏部侍郎。
Jingxiu passed the jinshi and entered by macro-phrase examination, appointed proofreader of the Secretariat, serving Xu Prefecture. Soon appointed vice magistrate of Weinan and collator of the Hall of Assembled Worthies. Transferred to Right Remonstrance Official and academician of the Hall of Assembled Worthies. He served in succession as Right Remonstrance Official, performed duties well, transferred to recorder of conduct, soon transferred to vice director in the Ministry of Rites. He entered as Hanlin academician, transferred to director in the Ministry of Rites, left office and returned to his post. Again transferred to director in the Ministry of War and drafter of edicts. When mourning ended after his father's death and service was complete, he was changed to vice director of the Ministry of Works, acting director of personnel selection, transferred to vice director of the Ministry of Personnel.
111
上將立魯王為太子，慎選師傅，改工部侍郎，兼魯王傅。 奏：「劍南西川、山南西道每年稅茶及除陌錢，舊例委度支巡院勾當，榷稅當司於上都召商人便換。 太和元年，戶部侍郎崔元略與西川節度使商量，取其穩便，遂奏請茶稅事使司自勾當，每年出錢四萬貫送省。 近年已來，不依元奏，三道諸色錢物，州府逗留，多不送省。 請取江西例，於歸州置巡院一所，自勾當收管諸色錢物送省，所冀免有逋懸。 欲令巡官李濆專往與德裕、遵古商量制置，續具奏聞。」 從之。 又奏：「兩川米價騰踴，百姓流亡。 請糶兩川闕官職田祿米，以救貧人。」 從之。 再為尚書左丞。 太和九年三月，卒於家。
The emperor was about to establish the Prince of Lu as Heir Apparent; tutors were carefully chosen and he was changed to vice director of the Ministry of Works and concurrently tutor to the Prince of Lu. He memorialized: "Jiannan West Circuit and Shannan West Circuit each year tax tea and removal-money; by old precedent the disbursement commissioner's touring office handled it, and the monopoly tax office at the capital summoned merchants for convenient exchange. In the first year of Taihe Vice Minister of Revenue Cui Yuanlue with the West Circuit military commissioner discussed and took what was stable, then memorialized that tea tax affairs should be handled by the circuit office itself, each year sending forty thousand strings to the central government. In recent years they have not followed the original memorial; the three circuits' various monies and goods have been detained by prefectures and not sent to the center. I request following the Jiangxi precedent, establishing one touring office at Guizhou to handle and collect all monies and goods and send them to the center, hoping to avoid arrears. I wish to send touring official Li Fen specially to discuss arrangements with Deyu and Zungu and then report fully in a memorial." The court approved. He again memorialized: "In the two circuits rice prices soar and common people flee. I request selling vacant official salary-field rice of the two circuits to aid the poor." The court approved. He again became Left Vice Director of the Secretariat. In the third month of the ninth year of Taihe he died at home.
112
敬休姿容溫雅，襟抱夷曠，不飲酒茹葷，不邇聲色。 著《諭善錄》七卷。 贈吏部尚書。
Jingxiu's bearing was warm and elegant, his mind broad and untroubled; he did not drink wine, eat meat, or approach music and women. He authored Exhortations to Goodness in seven scrolls. He was posthumously enfeoffed as minister of personnel.
113
辛讜
Xin Tan
114
辛讜，故太原尹雲京之孫，壽州刺史晦之猶子也。 性慷慨，重然諾，專務賑人之急。 年五十，不求茍進，有濟時匡難之志。
Xin Tan was grandson of Yunjing, former metropolitan magistrate of Taiyuan, and nephew of Hui, prefect of Shouzhou. By nature generous, he valued promises and specially devoted himself to relieving others' emergencies. At fifty he did not seek advancement by compromise; he had the will to aid the age and rescue difficulty.
115
咸通十年，龐勛亂徐泗。 時杜慆守泗州，賊以郡當江淮要害，極力攻之。 時兩淮郡縣皆陷。 慆守臨淮久之，援軍雖集，賊未解圍。 時讜寓居廣陵，乃仗劍拏小艇趨泗口，貫城柵入城見慆。 慆素聞有義而不相面，喜讜至，握手謝曰：「判官李延樞方話子為人，何遽至耶？ 吾無憂矣！」 時賊三面攻城，王師結壘於洪源驛。 相顧不前。 讜夜以小舟穿賊壘至洪源驛。 見監軍郭厚本，論泗州危急，且宜速救，厚本然之。 淮南都將王公弁謂厚本曰：「賊眾我寡，無宜輕舉，當俟可行。」 讜坐中拔劍瞋目謂公弁曰：「賊百道攻城，陷在旦夕。 公等奉詔赴援，而逗留不進，更欲何為？ 不唯有負國恩，丈夫氣義，亦宜感發！ 假如臨淮陷賊，淮南即是寇場，公何獨存耶！」 即欲揮刃向公弁，厚本持之。 讜望泗州大哭經日，帳下為之流涕。 厚本義其心，選勇士三百，隨讜入泗州。 夜半斬賊柵，大呼，由水門而入，賊軍大駭。 既知援兵入，賊乃退舍，人心遂固。
In the tenth year of Xiantong Pang Xun rebelled in Xu and Si. At that time Du Tao defended Sizhou; the rebels because the prefecture lay at the key point of the Jiang and Huai exerted extreme force attacking it. At that time the two Huai prefectures all fell. Tao held Linhuai for a long time; though relief armies gathered the rebels did not lift the siege. At that time Tan was lodging at Guangling; he then grasped sword, took a small boat, and hurried to Sizhou, piercing the city palisade to enter the city and see Tao. Tao had long heard of his righteousness but had never met him face to face; delighted at Tan's arrival he grasped his hand and thanked him: "Case officer Li Yanshu was just speaking of you—how did you come so swiftly? I have no worry!" At that time rebels attacked the city on three sides; imperial armies encamped at Hongyuan Station. They looked at each other and did not advance. Tan at night took a small boat through the rebel camp to Hongyuan Station. He saw Military Supervisor Guo Houben, discussed Sizhou's extreme peril, and that relief should be swift; Houben agreed. Huainan general Wang Gongbian told Houben, "Rebel forces are many, ours few—no light move should be made; we should wait until action is feasible." Tan in the gathering drew sword, glared, and told Gongbian, "The rebels attack the city on a hundred paths; capture is imminent. You all received orders to aid—yet linger without advancing; what more do you intend? Not only do you fail national grace—a man's righteous spirit should also be stirred! If Linhuai falls to rebels, Huainan becomes the bandits' battlefield—why do you alone preserve yourself!" He was about to swing the blade at Gongbian; Houben restrained him. Tan faced Sizhou and wept all day; those in the tent wept for him. Houben respected his heart and selected three hundred brave men to follow Tan into Sizhou. At midnight they cut the rebel palisade, shouted loudly, and entered through the water gate; rebel troops were greatly alarmed. Once they knew relief troops had entered, the rebels then withdrew; hearts in the city were thereby strengthened.
116
浙西觀察使杜審權遣大將翟行約率軍三千赴援，屯蓮塘驛。 慆欲遣人勞之，將吏皆憚其行。 讜曰：「杜相公以大夫宗盟，急難相赴，安得令使者無言而還！」 即賫慆書幣，犒其使。 淮南大將李湘率師五千來援，賊詐降，敗於淮口，湘與郭厚本皆為賊所執，自是無援。 賊並兵急攻，以鐵鎖斷淮流，梯沖雲合，凡周七月，晝夜不息。 乘城之士，不遑寢寐，面目生瘡，軍儲漸少，分食稀粥。 賴讜犯難仗義，求救於淮北諸軍。 既而馬舉以大軍至，賊解圍而去。
Zhexi Observation Commissioner Du Shenquan dispatched great general Zhai Xingyue leading three thousand troops to aid, encamped at Liantang Station. Tao wished to send men to comfort them; generals and officials all feared the journey. Tan said, "Vice Minister Du, as a senior clansman in urgent difficulty, came to aid—how can we let the envoy return without a word!" He then bore Tao's letter and gifts and rewarded the envoy. Huainan great general Li Xiang led five thousand troops to aid; the rebels feigned surrender and were defeated at Huaikou; Xiang and Guo Houben were both seized by rebels—thereafter there was no relief. Rebels combined forces for urgent attack, using iron chains to block the Huai current; scaling ladders and assault engines converged like clouds—for a full seven weeks day and night without cease. Those who manned the walls had no time to sleep; faces grew sores; military stores gradually dwindled and they divided thin porridge. They relied on Tan braving hardship and upholding righteousness to beg rescue from armies north of the Huai. Soon Ma Ju arrived with a great army and the rebels lifted the siege and departed.
117
讜無子，猶子山僧、元老等寄在廣陵。 每出城，則書二姓名，謂慆曰：「誌之，得嗣為幸。」 慆益感之。 賊平，授讜泗州團練判官、侍御史。 慆遷鄭滑節度，讜亦從之，為賓佐。 慆卒，乃退歸江東，以隱居為事。
Tan had no sons; nephews the monk Shanseng, Yuangao, and others were lodged at Guangling. Each time he left the city he wrote two names and told Tao, "Record them—if descendants result, it is fortune." Tao was the more moved. When rebels were pacified Tan was appointed regimental adjutant of Sizhou and attendant censor. Tao transferred to Zheng and Hua military commission; Tan also followed as staff member. When Tao died he then retired to Jiangdong and made seclusion his occupation.
118
贊
Commentary:
119
贊曰：獸解觸邪，草能指佞。 烈士徇義，見危致命。 國有忠臣，亡而復存。 何以喪邦？ 奸邪受恩。
Beasts can gore evil; grass can point at flatterers. Martyr-scholars follow righteousness, seeing peril and giving life. When a state has loyal ministers, though perished it is as if alive. How is a state lost? Wicked and treacherous receive favor.
